Statement 
The Law Commission of India has submitted its 173rd report on Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 
2000. According to the Law Commission the draft bill seeks to provide Law enforcement agencies 
with suitable powers to deal effectively with the growing menace of terrorism in the country and 
also contains provisions for checking misuse of powers by the investigating agencies. 
The salient features of the Bill include a comprehensive definition of terrorist acts, provisions 
for seizure, attachment and forfeiture of proceeds of terrorism; provisions for expeditious trial by 
special courts and protection of witnesses; inve stigation by office not below the rank of Deputy 
Superintendent of Police or equivalent as also adverse inference as to accused in certain cases. 
Suitable safeguards against abuse of various provisions have been provided including confirmation 
of detention by Director General of Police an d State Review Committees within ten and thirty 
days respectively, etc. 
The Government has invited the views of the all the State Government/UT administrations on 
the various provisions of the bill. The Government will hold consultations with political parties 
and other concerned agencies/groups before taking a final view.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI I.D. SWAMI): 
(a) and (b) Home Secretary leve l talks were held in Kathma ndu from July 4.7.2000. At this 
meeting the two sides discussed modalities to e nhance cooperation in combating activities of 
terrorist, criminal and other undersirable el ements, including along th e India-Nepal border. 
Cooperation between the law enforcement agen cies of both the countries and improved 
management of the India-Nepal border were also discussed. 
(c) it was agreed to further intensify coopera tion and jointly coordina te measures, including 
stepping up vigil along the contiguous border distri cts of India and Nepal, to counter activities 
inimical to India's interests. Shared concern on  this matter was evident from the determination 
expressed by both sides to take  urgent necessary steps to control misuse of the open border 
between the two countries. It was also agreed to introduce with effect from October 1,2000, a 
"pruned down" list of photo identification documents  that would be valid for air travel by India

investment towards increasing co al production in the 24 sub-projec t under five subsidiaries i.e. 
Central coalfields Limited (CCL), Mahanadi Co alfields Limited (MCL), Western Coalfields

institutional capacity development in the project implementation, mining operations and 
management.

1181, SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: W ill the Minister of NON-CONVENTIONAL 
ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Solar Energy Programme is regarded- as one of the World's 
largest programme, if so, the countries which; are following the similar kind of programmes; 
(b) what 'are the highlights of the Solar Energy Programme in other countries;  
(c) if the programme. is commercially viable in  other countries, what, is the.cost incurred 
thereon; and 
(d.) what is: the difference in the level of technologies used in India and other countries? 
134 

 137
 [2 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-CONVENTIONAL  ENERGY 
SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) Th e Indian "solar energy programme is 
regarded as one of the largest national programmes in the world in this field. Other, countries 
which have policies to support solar energy deve lopment as well as major programmes in solar 
photovoltaic and thermal technologies  include USA, Japan, Germany,  China, Australia, France, 
Netherlands, Austria, Israel, Italy and Spain. 
USA is pursuing the development and utilization of a variety of solar technologies for a large 
number of applications. A programme for the installation of 1 miltidtt solar systems on roof-tops 
of houses and Other buildings was announced in 1997. This includes solar photovoltaic systems 
for electricity generation as well as solar thermal systems for water heating. In Germany, a new 
programme for 100,000 solar roofs was launche d in 1999. About 33,000 roof-top photovoltaic; 
systems have been installed in Japan till March 2000 under its national programme. In Israel, 
legislation has made it mandatory to install sola r water heaters in several types of buildings 
including most residential utitis. Megawatt- size power plants based on solar thermal and 
photovoltaic technologies have been installed in USA. Photovotaic power plants have also been 
installed for purposes of demonstration and evalua tion in several other countries including Italy, 
Germany and Japan, Research and development is also being suppor ted in Japan, USA,.Australia 
and several European countries. 
(c) The commercial viability of any solar energy system depends on a number of factors such as 
the solar radiation level, load, c onsumption pattern and the availabili ty and cost of electricity or 
fossil fuels. The cost of electricity from solar thermal or photovoltaic sy stems is generally not 
competitive to that: generated from conventional energy sources. The megawatt-size power plants 
abroad have been built either under government-funded demonstration programmes or by 
availing of special tax benefits and other ince ntives. The solar roof programme in Japan is 
supported by government subsidies; in Germany it is supported by soft loans.and a special price 
for the electricity supplied to the grid by hous e owners. The international price for photovoltaic 
modules is around $ 4 per watt and the cost of electricity for stand-alone systems varies between 
135 

 138
RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2000] 
25 to 50 cents per kilowatt hour. However, photo voltaic power can be economical in remote and 
unelectrified areas and for small power applications, as is also the case in India. 
Solar water heating systems for household use are c onsidered to be commercially viable in most 
countries including India. The cost of a solar water hearing system of 100—120 litre capacity 
varies between $ 400—600. Industrial and institutional solar water heating systems are 
competitive only if the alternative is electricity or a high-priced fuel. 
(d) As a result of development and commercialisation efforts made during the past two decades, a 
substantial base for the manufac ture of solar photovoltaic and solar thermal products has been 
established in India. Almost the entire production of solar cells in India is based on the single 
crystal silicon technology. Technologies such  as multi-crystalline silicon, amorphous silicon and 
other thin film solar cells which account for over 60% of the world's production are not yet in 
commercial production in India. Nevertheless, so lar cells and modules made in India are being 
exported to several countries abroad. Solar collector material for thermal applications is also being 
exported from India. Several Indian companies have obtained the ISO 9000 quality certification. 
The main difference in the production of solar pr oducts in India and some other countries lies in 
the volume of production and the range of techno logies employed. Lead ing foreign companies 
have production capacities which ar e 5 to 10 times that of Indian companies. A higher level of 
automation is also seen in foreign manufacturing organizations.

(a) whether Government have received the recommendations from the institution of Engineers

Mangement Programme include ins itu soil-moisture conservation, checking of land degradation

Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), National Waters hed Development Project for Rainfed Areas

catchment of River Valley Projects & Flood Prone Rivers (RVP & FPR). Under NWDPRA.

area has been developed in the last three years.  Under IWDP, ten projects  have been sanctioned

under implementation in 16 districts. In these di stricts, 699 watershed projects covering an area 
of about 3.5 lakhs ha. are presently under impl ementation. A project under IWDP is generally 
evaluated after the release of 45% of the project costs. The task of evaluation of RVP & FPR

Compensation to Kuwait Evacuees 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, during the Iraq-Kuwait war, thousands of 
Indians working in Kuwait were evacuated. Ther eafter, a United Nations Claims Commission 
was established at Geneva to compensate the vi ctims who lost their earnings and savings due to 
the war. The victims were asked to send their claims for compensation to the United Nations 
Claims Commission (UNCC) through their respec tive Governments. In India, the Special 
Kuwait Cell coordinated and monitored the pro cessing of applications and disbursement of 
compensation. Accordingly, the Government of India, as per the decision of the UNCC, received 
applications for claims until 1991 and extended the time thereafter upto 1992. Corresponding to 
these dates, the victims had sent their applications. The Government of India notified a proforma 
in newspapers for submitting their claims. Howeve r, most of the victims of the evacuation are 
illiterate labourers and not well educated and they  could not have read the newspapers. Hence, 
they were not aware of the new procedures that have been adopted and they could not send their 
applications in the new proforma. However, the applications which were sent in plain papers 
were rejected and the victims were denied the compensation with the sole reason that they failed 
to apply in the appropriate format. All th ese victims are sufferi ng from utter poverty and 
unemployment. They are not even able to meet their needs and have two meals a day. Sir, 
thousands of workers from my district, Cuddapah,  in Andhra Pradesh are being denied of this 
compensation amount. They are unable to come over to Delhi and stay here for some days for 
this purpose. It is a costly affair to them; he nce most of the people could not come. However, 
even in the case of those people who managed to come over here, the Kuwaiti Embassy officials 
are not even giving appointments to them as their names are not included in the list of eligible 
persons for receiving the compensation. Consider ing this miserable condi tion of the people, I 
request the Government to consider their applications sympathetically and grant the 
compensation which is legitimately due to them.

Before replying to the specific points raised by  the Members of Parliament, I would like to give 
some background to the repeal of these two laws. 
The Department of Administrative Reforms had set up a Commission under the chairmanship of 
Shri P.C. Jain, in May, 1998, to review the laws and regulations, id entifying proposals for 
amendments to the existing laws and to make recommendations for repeal/amendment of the 
laws. 
The Commission has identified certain laws which are no longer relevant and, therefore, can be 
repealed. For the steel sector, the laws identified are: 
(1) The Iron & Steel Company (Taking over of Management) Act, 1972. 
(2) The Iron & Steel Companies (Amalgamation) Act, 1952. 
The Iron and Steel Companies (Amalgamation) Act, 1952 (Act No.79 of 1952) was enacted to 
amalgamate the Indian Iron & Steel Company Limited with the Steel Corporation of Bengal on 
the recommendation of the Tariff 
245 

 
RAJYA SABHA      [02 August, 2000] 
Board and the Tariff Commission. In the initia l years, after independence, when a serious 
shortage of steel was hampering the nation-building activities, it became imperative to eliminate 
duplication and waste and, ultimately, reduce the co st of production of steel. For this purpose, it 
was thought fit that the Stee! Corporation of Be ngal Limited, which had its works at Kulti, 
District Burdwan, West Bengal and the Indi an Iron and Steel Company Limited, Burnpur, 
District Burdwan, West Bengal, both of which were enga ged in the manufacture and production 
of iron and steel, should be amalgamated. The amalgamation was thought necessary to give effect 
to the schemes of the Centra! Government for expansion of the iron and steel industry and to 
make resources available for such expansion. 
The Act has now served its purpose, and no action might have been left over, which has to be 
undertaken under or in accordance with the provisions  of the said Act. It is, therefore, no more 
necessary to retain this Act on the Statute Book. 
Secondly, in accordance with the previsions of  the Indian Iron and Steel Company (Taking over 
of Management) Act, 1972 the ma nagement of Indian Iron and Steel Company was taken over 
initially for a period of two years, w.e.f. 14.7.1972, to secure its proper management. The period 
was extended for five years to co mplete restructuring and to streamline the administrative set-up 
of the Company. The said period of five years expired on 15 ,h July, 1977. Consequently, the Act 
is no longer operative. Subsequently, the Indian Iron and Steel Company (Acquisition of Shares) 
Act, 1976 was passed and the company was completely nationalised. In 1978, IISCO became a 
subsidiary of SAIL under the Public Sector iron and Steel Copmpanies (Restructuring) and 
Miscellaneous Act of 1978. Thus,. the Act, having  seized its purpose, is no longer operative and 
can be removed from the Statute book. 
As I have explained, I again state that thes e Acts have no relevance now and are in no way 
connected with the restructuring of SAIL or w ith the proposed conversion of IISCO into a joint 
venture, which is under the consideration of the Government. 
Madam, these two Acts are completely redundant now and they are no more operative. Hence, I 
request the hon. Members to support the passage of this Bill.

ship to mouth, is today wholly self-sufficient in basic foodgrains, is a tribute to our farming

a fact that there are basic structural maladies which still persist.

When India became independent, our agriculture  accounted for 50% of our national income. It 
accounted for 70% of our population, In the last 50 years, because of occupational 
diversification, the share of agriculture in the national income of our country has gone down 
from 50% to 28%. But the share of agricultural population in the lotal population has come down 
only from 70% to 65%. We, therefore, have a situation now where 50% of the national income

people dependent on agriculture has not declined as a result, The disparity in incomes between

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Incidence of killing by the Militants in Jammu and Kashmir on the intervening night of 1st 
and 2nd August, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS {SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Madam, a series of ghastly 
incidents perpetrated by militants, taking a toll of  as many as 80 lives,  have been reported from 
Jammu and Kashmir on the 
night of r: and 2'''' August, 2000. 
In the first incident, at about 18-45 hours on 1 SI August, a group of terrorists fired 
indiscriminately at Pahalgam where Amarnath Ya tris were camping. The incident took place 
across Lidder Nallah on the road leading to Aroo when terrorists fired at two Langars and CRPF 
personnel. The firing was retaliated by the CRP F. 27 persons, including two police personnel, 
have been killed and 50 injured. Two militants re sponsible for the firing were also killed on the 
spot. From them, the following recoveries have been effected: AK Rifles-2, AK Magazines- 19, 
Rifie grenades--8, Hand-grenades--2, Grenade launcher-1, Rounds-55, Transistor--1.

RAJYA SABHA      [02 August, 2000] 
In the second and third incidents, the militants had attacked two brick ki ln labour camps, one at 
Mir Bazar, Quazigund in Anantnag District, the other at Mir Nowgam (Achhabal). 19 labourers 
were killed at Mir Bazar and 7 labourers at Mir Nowgam. During the same night, in Pogal 
Paristan in Ramban area (Doda District), anot her group of militants killed 14 persons. In the 
same district in village Keyar, eight members of a village defence committee were killed by 
terrorists. The sixth incident took place at Kalaroos (Kupwara district) where five members of a 
Muslim family were massacred. 
The Stale Government has initiated precautionary and relief measures. Special Secretary in the 
Department of J and K Affairs,  along with DG, CRPF have been deputed to J and K to review 
the situation and the security arrangements along with the security forces in the field. 
Consequent on the cease-fire declaration made by the Hizbul Muzahideen and the Government's 
positive response to this offer, th ere have been reports that some of the other militant outfits, 
with a large component of foreign mercenaries,  who were unhappy about the offer of Hizbul 
Mujahideen, may create problems and escalate violence. The security forces had been alerted of 
this and have been asked to be more vigilant. II is because of this vigilance that the security 
forces had foiled an atternpt of the militants to attack the Amarnath pilgrims in a Jammu camp 
on the morning of 1st August. In this clash, one militant was killed and another injured. 
No words would be too strong to condemn these outrageous incidents of violence which are no 
doubt part of the continuing proxy war being wa ged against us by a hostile neighbour. But the 
Government feels that this latest  outburst of violence is also a determined bid by those upset at 
the prospects of peace to abort the initiative taken by the Hizbul Mujahideen last week. 
The Government is determined to continue the Amarnath Yatra with renewed security measures 
and to provide all necessary protection to the common people. Besides, the Government will 
persevere in its efforts to bring normalcy to th e State of Jammu and Ka shmir by engaging in a 
dialogue with the peace-loving people.
